title: Why avoid slow network calls inside a TX? Why can the pool exhaust even when DB is healthy? Why does 200 Tomcat threads + 10 HikariCP connections = "DB fast but app slow"? Why is increasing pool the wrong fix?
keyPoints: A @Transactional method holds a database connection for its entire duration, including non-DB work like REST calls
A 3-second REST call inside a TX wastes the connection for 3 seconds of idle time on the DB side
200 Tomcat threads competing for 10 HikariCP connections means 190 threads block waiting for a connection
SQL takes 5 ms but the user sees 500 ms because 495 ms is spent waiting for a free connection
Increasing the pool size is the wrong fix because it pushes more concurrent load onto the database
The correct fix is short transactions with DB-only work, external calls moved outside the TX, and pool sized to DB capacity

s1_definition.oneliner: A @Transactional method holds a database connection for its entire duration, so a slow network call inside the transaction wastes the connection and starves other threads, causing pool exhaustion even when the database itself is healthy.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Connection holding** -- a `@Transactional` method checks out a connection from HikariCP at begin and does not release it until commit or rollback, tying the connection to the entire method body.
- **Idle waste** -- if you make a 3-second REST call inside the TX, the connection sits idle on the database side but is counted as in-use by the pool.
- **Thread-pool mismatch** -- 200 Tomcat worker threads competing for 10 HikariCP connections means at most 10 threads do DB work at once while 190 block inside `getConnection()`.
- **False bottleneck** -- SQL runs in 5 ms but latency reaches 500 ms because the time is spent waiting for a free connection, not running queries.
- **Wrong fix** -- increasing the pool to 200 pushes 200 concurrent sessions onto the database, overwhelming its CPU and lock manager.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, each teller window has its own cash drawer (connection). Rajesh is at a window processing a transfer for Priya, but in the middle he picks up the phone and makes a 3-minute call to an insurance company. His window is blocked the whole time even though the cash drawer is idle. Meanwhile, 190 customers stand in line. The cash drawers are fine, the vault is fast, but service is terrible because windows are occupied by people on the phone. Adding more windows (connections) just means more tellers on the phone at once, overwhelming the vault.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A database connection is held for the entire duration of a @Transactional method. If you place a 3-second REST call inside the transaction, the connection sits idle on the database side for 3 seconds while being counted as in-use by the pool. With 10 connections and 3-second calls, maximum throughput drops to roughly 3 requests per second. The classic symptom is the "DB fast but app slow" mystery: SQL takes 5 milliseconds but the user sees 500 milliseconds because 495 milliseconds is spent waiting for a free connection from an exhausted pool.

The instinctive fix of increasing the pool size is wrong. Matching the pool to 200 Tomcat threads pushes 200 concurrent sessions onto the database, overwhelming its CPU and lock manager. You trade "app slow" for "DB slow." The HikariCP documentation quotes the PostgreSQL team's formula: connections equal core count times two plus effective spindle count, which often lands at 10 to 20 connections.

The correct fix is keeping transactions short with only database operations inside them. Move external calls outside the transaction using Spring events or the outbox pattern. Use `LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy` to defer connection acquisition until the first SQL statement. Monitor `hikaricp.connections.pending` in Grafana and alert when threads start waiting.

Remember one sentence: keep transactions short and network-free, because the connection is held for the entire method, not just the SQL.
